a_rows_sample.anchor: Q1 — what problem was the model created to solve? ... "this model says what decisions an Engineer resolves with them"
a_rows_sample.statement: The Engineering Decision Model was created because standards say what the rules are, while the model says what decisions an engineer resolves with them: rules existed but the decisions they answer were unindexed. Its anti-problem: it is a decision INDEX, never a second rulebook (ARB, 2026-07-11) — created to prevent duplicated authority, not to add a layer. Its birth act included a vocabulary correction (2026-07-11): a DDD Domain Service is executable, a decision is a specification. Its adoption bar: one real engineering cycle must show consistent resolution through the model; it is DRAFT until earned.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q2 — which decisions does it explicitly model? ... Eight — all of one family
a_rows_sample.statement: Eight decisions are explicitly modeled, all of one family (the flow of knowledge and artifacts through governed work), grouped by question: 'Where does it belong?' (DetermineConcern, DeterminePlacement - mechanized by doc-placement.php); 'What is it/does it live?' (DetermineArtifactLifecycle - deletion litmus, DetermineArtifactType); 'Is it worth keeping/raising?' (DetermineReusePotential - Harvest, DeterminePromotionPath - ladder entry); 'What governs/verifies it?' (DetermineApplicableStandards, DetermineQualificationMethod). Deliberately excluded: ADR-making, capability approval, authority acts, promotion rulings — 'promotion is a human governance act and is never automated'; 'the AI evaluates and recommends — authority remains with governance.' The absence of governance decisions from the catalog is design, not gap.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q3 — which discovered decisions are not represented? ... FREEZE and RETIRE extend nothing in the catalog
a_rows_sample.statement: Answered in a prior Discovery pass and carried forward unchanged: FREEZE (n>=3, undeclared authority) and RETIRE (PM-6) extend nothing in the catalog, submitted as insufficiency evidence per the model's own stopping rule. Implicit but exercised: the challenge-commissioning trigger and terminology adoption. Nothing further found in this pass, which per the stopping rule is the correct amount.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q4 — does it govern the full ladder, or only architecture decisions? ... NEITHER — and the answer is the INVERSE of the commission's suspicion
a_rows_sample.statement: The model governs zero architecture decisions (no DetermineArchitectureDecision exists; ADRs are governance acts, outside the catalog by design). What it governs on the ladder Observation->Hypothesis->Evidence->Principle->Architecture is the entry points, not the rungs: DetermineReusePotential opens the ladder (observation->candidate); DeterminePromotionPath routes onto it (candidate->pilot->qualification->ARB decides). The rungs belong to ES-006.1, and the model correctly refuses to own them since it is an index, never a second rulebook.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q5 — Knowledge Governance or only Engineering Governance? ... Engineering Governance NOW; Knowledge Governance ANTICIPATED
a_rows_sample.statement: The model's own Decision Catalogs table states Engineering Standards answer the catalog's Engineering Decisions, while Project-Knowledge-class Knowledge Decisions (DetermineKnowledgeNeed, Source, Representation, Qualification, Promotion) are 'pilot-gated candidates — arrive only with pilot evidence; same pattern, different domain.' Engineering Governance is present now; Knowledge Governance is anticipated with the arrival condition already stated, and the entire ontology/meta-model corpus of this programme is exactly the kind of pilot evidence the anticipated catalog says it is waiting for.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q6 — extend the model, or map onto it? ... MAP. Tested element by element
a_rows_sample.statement: Ontology/meta-model elements map onto the existing decision model rather than extending it: archetype classification extends DetermineArtifactType (same question, richer vocabulary); KNOWLEDGE != ARTIFACT (I-1) is presupposed by DetermineArtifactLifecycle's deletion litmus; AUTHORITY-SCOPE/CONTAINER boundary maps to DetermineConcern/DeterminePlacement; GOVERNANCE-STATUS/EVIDENCE-STATUS maps to DeterminePromotionPath; NATURE (normative force) maps to DetermineApplicableStandards. Nothing in the ontology requires a new decision; the only extension pressure (FREEZE/RETIRE) is not ontology-driven, but comes from the enacted governance record. Verdict: the ontology supplies the vocabulary the catalog's procedures presuppose; the catalog supplies the purpose the ontology elements must serve — they interlock, neither extends the other.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q7 — would a second decision model violate ubiquitous language? ... YES — three times over
a_rows_sample.statement: A second decision model would violate ubiquitous language three times over: (1) the model's charter states it is 'a decision INDEX, never a second rulebook' — a v2 is exactly what it exists to prevent; (2) I-5, lint-enforced, requires one authoritative artifact per topic+context, so a second model is a literal violation; (3) ES-005.4 requires one rule -> one home. A competing 'KnowledgeOS Decision Model' would have been the UL violation and was not created; the Discovery and Validation passes are readings of the one model, not rivals to it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: U-EDV-1 | Does the DA intend the anticipated PKS-class Knowledge Decision catalog (§5) to be the home of the knowledge-governance decisions this programme surfaced?
a_rows_sample.statement: U-EDV-1: does the Decision Authority intend the anticipated PKS-class Knowledge Decision catalog to be the home of the knowledge-governance decisions this programme surfaced — waits on the ARB, natural companion to D-8.

a_rows_sample.anchor: U-EDV-2 | The model's adoption test (one real cycle of conscious use) — unevenly met (U-DM-4, carried)
a_rows_sample.statement: U-EDV-2: the model's adoption test (one real cycle of conscious use) is unevenly met (U-DM-4, carried forward), waiting on EP-02 of the next real cycle.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DP-n as a distinct layer between principle and capability ... UNIQUE HYPOTHESIS — needs operational proof
a_rows_sample.statement: DP-n as a distinct architectural layer between principle and capability has no direct external counterpart found (policy-as-code practice is only adjacent); it remains a unique hypothesis requiring operational proof.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Canonical concept glossary — the 14 examined, plus 3 the corpus forces in
a_rows_sample.statement: A 17-row glossary assigns each term (KnowledgeOS, PKS, Engineering Knowledge, Engineering Capability, Engineering Method, Engineering Governance, Engineering Runtime, Runtime Adapter, Engineering Evidence, Engineering Ontology, Documentation Ontology L-A, Platform Ontology L-B, Product Ontology L-C, Knowledge Graph, Engineering Kernel, Knowledge Space, Design Policy DP-n, Execution Asset AST-nnn) one meaning, owner, protected invariant, place, and verdict (KEEP/REJECTED-MERGED/SPLIT/CANDIDATE). Success criterion: every major engineering term gets one meaning, one owner, one place.

a_rows_sample.anchor: RESULT: THE MODEL DOES NOT SURVIVE INTACT. One claim FALSIFIED · two WEAKENED · two SURVIVED · two unchanged
a_rows_sample.statement: Overall falsification result: of the domain model's claims, one is falsified, two weakened, two survived, two unchanged; the strongest claim in the model (D-2) was among those weakened, by evidence the model itself had cited. Method: every test executed against artifacts, not reasoned from the model, using the repository's own instruments (Round47-OP's nine admissible justifications, the R16 Workbook Strong/Medium/Weak scale); four falsifiers were sought, three landed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: W-1 · D-2's "own decision series" is a shared authority — two of four grounds fall
a_rows_sample.statement: D-2's claim of 'its own decision series, ADR-M distinct from ADR-AIP' is weakened: Round39-D6's header states decision authority for all ADRs is 'sponsor + ARB' and amendment requires sponsor+ARB approval, so ADR-M is a scoping device under a shared authority, not a separate authority. Its claim of 'independent evolution' is falsified: Round39-D6 states the ADRs 'were authored together on 2026-06-25' — a series written in one sitting evidences independent subject, never independent evolution over time. This matches the ARB Chair's named falsifier 'ADR separation is historical rather than semantic' — half true: separation is real in subject, absent in time.

a_rows_sample.anchor: S-1 · D-2 survives on a ground I had not weighted — an explicit mutual scope exclusion
a_rows_sample.statement: D-2 survives on a new ground: Round39-D6's verbatim rule 'Governance discoveries (constitutional/capability) MUST NOT appear here. No DDD concepts here' is a deliberately maintained boundary (not an accident of filing), bidirectional in effect (ADR-M excludes governance, ADR-AIP carries no methodology rules), and survives the shared-authority finding since a shared authority that forbids itself from mixing two subjects is evidence FOR two models, not against. D-2 remains a boundary, but on subject exclusion, not on decision-series separation or independent evolution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: S-3 · D-1 survives every falsifier
a_rows_sample.statement: D-1 survives every falsifier sought: no multiple owners of the same concept found (DA/ARB throughout), no changes that fail to co-occur (ES set moves under STANDARDS_INDEX), no forced co-evolution with a product (ratification and freeze are product-independent), no absent invariants (append-only rulings, R-46).

a_rows_sample.anchor: U-1 | Was Round39-MC adopted by sponsor authority BECAUSE D-2 is independent, or DESPITE it being part of D-1?
a_rows_sample.statement: U-1: was Round39-MC adopted because D-2 is independent, or despite it being part of D-1 — the artifacts record the act but never the reason; only the sponsor and ARB know, and the model's validity turns on it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: U-4 | Is Round39-D6's scope exclusion still enforced, or was it stated once?
a_rows_sample.statement: U-4: is Round39-D6's scope exclusion still enforced or was it stated once — stated 2026-06-25, no subsequent enforcement event found.

a_rows_sample.anchor: U-6 | Does D-1 authorize D-2, or are they peers?
a_rows_sample.statement: U-6: does D-1 authorize D-2, or are they peers — carried forward, now sharper: shared ARB suggests peers-under-one-authority, not hierarchy.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Confidence — R16 Workbook scale, scored independently ... falsified ≠ unevidenced
a_rows_sample.statement: Per-domain confidence after falsification (R16 Strong/Medium/Weak scale): D-1 Strong->STRONG; D-2 Strong->MEDIUM; D-3 Strong->WEAK; D-6a (Evidence Protocol) new->MEDIUM; D-6b (Product Evidence) new->STRONG; D-5 (Engineering Capability, not a context) Medium->MEDIUM (unchanged, H-CAT-1 stands); D-4 (Workflow, rejected) ->STRONG as a rejection; D-7 (PKS, a context type) new->WEAK. Distinction drawn: falsified is worse than unevidenced — D-3 and D-7 carry contradicting evidence (falsified); D-6a carries no evidence (unevidenced).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Recommendation — per domain ... The model as a whole | REVISE, then re-test ... NOT canonical
a_rows_sample.statement: Per-domain recommendations: D-1 ACCEPT; D-2 REVISE (restate the boundary on the one surviving ground, Round39-D6's scope exclusion; delete 'own decision series' and 'independent evolution' as grounds); D-3 DEFER (untestable at n=1, revisit when a second runtime adapter exists); D-6a DEFER, D-6b ACCEPT; D-5 ACCEPT the demotion (do not promote until ARB overturns H-CAT-1 on evidence); D-4 ACCEPT the rejection; D-7 REVISE (restate as an observation of one instance, record PKS-as-projection as falsified). Overall the model as a whole: REVISE then re-test, NOT canonical — 2 of 8 accept, 3 revise, 2 defer, 1 accept-as-rejection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Q6 — extend the model, or map onto it? ... MAP. Tested element by element
b_rows_sample.statement: Ontology/meta-model elements map onto the existing decision model rather than extending it: archetype classification extends DetermineArtifactType (same question, richer vocabulary); KNOWLEDGE != ARTIFACT (I-1) is presupposed by DetermineArtifactLifecycle's deletion litmus; AUTHORITY-SCOPE/CONTAINER boundary maps to DetermineConcern/DeterminePlacement; GOVERNANCE-STATUS/EVIDENCE-STATUS maps to DeterminePromotionPath; NATURE (normative force) maps to DetermineApplicableStandards. Nothing in the ontology requires a new decision; the only extension pressure (FREEZE/RETIRE) is not ontology-driven, but comes from the enacted governance record. Verdict: the ontology supplies the vocabulary the catalog's procedures presuppose; the catalog supplies the purpose the ontology elements must serve — they interlock, neither extends the other.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X-3 | ontology governance practice (OBO-style community ownership, versioning) — challenges individual ownership of a governed vocabulary
b_rows_sample.statement: Challenge X-3: OBO-style community-ownership ontology-governance practice challenges the platform's individual ownership of a governed vocabulary. Bears on SC-2/D-6.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ⛔ Engineering Ontology | REJECTED — merges into Documentation Ontology. L-A already covers engineering-knowledge kinds; a fourth layer was declined on evidence
b_rows_sample.statement: 'Engineering Ontology' as a distinct concept is rejected and merges into Documentation Ontology (L-A), since L-A already covers engineering-knowledge kinds; a proposed fourth ontology layer was declined for lack of evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: U-MM-5 | The three formal meta-artifacts (RQ-002 · the Metamodel · this discovery) must not become a fourth unreconciled ontology
b_rows_sample.statement: U-MM-5: the three formal meta-artifacts (RQ-002, the Metamodel, this Discovery) must not become a fourth unreconciled ontology; this document is input to D-8's reconciliation, never a competitor.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 2. CANDIDATE — supported by evidence, awaiting ruling or more evidence (K-1..K-15)
b_rows_sample.statement: Fifteen candidate concerns, each citing its supporting commission and what it waits on: K-1 dimensional-with-archetypes meta-model; K-2 the archetype set (strong: DOMAIN/PROCESS/CAPABILITY/KNOWLEDGE/ARTIFACT/RUNTIME ASSET/PROJECTION; weaker: CONTAINER; weakest: PURPOSE); K-3 the four partial orders (authority, production, realization, containment); K-4 11 invariant relationships vs 8 implementation choices; K-5 DP-n as capability anchor; K-6 Knowledge Space = declared boundary+owner+constitution; K-7 authority = provenance x standing, four progression kinds; K-8 the strategic domain set PD-1/2/3/5; K-9 viewpoints as presentation; K-10 decision-readiness as the platform's product; K-11 FREEZE/RETIRE as insufficiency evidence; K-12 PKS extends context-engineering with governance; K-13 the canon-track reference artifacts themselves; K-14 the mission is enacted via 8 artifacts; K-15 ownership splits (candidate-unowned=ladder working, operating-unowned=defect, sole instance Runtime Adapter).

b_rows_sample.anchor: THE CRITIQUE CORRECTS MY OWN RECOMMENDATION, AND IT IS RIGHT ... I recommended "express D-1..D-7 in knowledge-types.yaml." That mixes abstraction levels
b_rows_sample.statement: A prior recommendation to express D-1..D-7 (Engineering Governance etc.) in knowledge-types.yaml is withdrawn: it mixed abstraction levels, since Engineering Governance is not a document; the repository supplies mechanical, not merely aesthetic, proof (section 3).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Ontology scope — per schema file, as parsed ... THE 13% COVERAGE IS A DECLARED BOUNDARY, NOT AN OVERSIGHT
b_rows_sample.statement: Every schema file (knowledge-schema.yaml the metamodel with 16 fields/18 rules; knowledge-types.yaml 31 document types; knowledge-relationships.yaml 11 typed edges + 4 shortcuts, none expressing governs/produces/consumes/observes; statuses.yaml 8 lifecycle states; authorities.yaml 5 trust levels; knowledge-audiences.yaml 9 audiences; bounded-contexts.yaml 12 product contexts) was parsed with the repository's own YAML loader. Finding: the graph's ~13% document coverage is a declared scope (scope.include: docs/knowledge/**/*.md), not an oversight — extending it would amend a declared scope, a governance act, not fix a bug.

b_rows_sample.anchor: knowledge-types.yaml IS a documentation ontology — I checked the temptation to call it a hybrid, and it is not one ... These are documents ABOUT domain objects
b_rows_sample.statement: knowledge-types.yaml is confirmed as a documentation ontology, not a hybrid: types like 'aggregate' or 'event' look like domain objects but their own descriptions are documentary ('aggregate' = a single aggregate's design, invariants, and boundary; 'event' = a domain event's payload/producers/consumers) — these are documents about domain objects, not the domain objects themselves.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Ontology layers — THREE, not four ... a fourth layer is therefore declined ... L-A EXISTS · EXECUTABLE · ENFORCED ... L-B DOES NOT EXIST ... L-C PARTIALLY EXISTS ... "Engineering Knowledge Ontology" NOT EVIDENCED AS A SEPARATE LAYER
b_rows_sample.statement: Three ontology layers are recognized, per the commission's own rule (do not invent new layers unless repository evidence requires them): L-A Documentation Ontology exists, executable, enforced (31 types x 8 statuses x 5 authorities x 9 audiences x 12 contexts x 11 edges, 18 lint rules, a generated graph); L-B Platform Ontology does not exist (D-1..D-7 is its seed); L-C Product Ontology partially exists (bounded-contexts.yaml plus unindexed Round29 catalogs). A proposed fourth 'Engineering Knowledge Ontology' middle layer is declined as not evidenced separately: knowledge-types.yaml already covers engineering-knowledge kinds (adr, ddd-discovery, research, review, playbook, checklist, template, decision, quality) — L-A is the engineering-knowledge ontology, at document granularity.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three independent proofs that D-1..D-7 do not belong in the existing schemas ... KEY COLLISION — mechanical, not aesthetic
b_rows_sample.statement: Three independent proofs that D-1..D-7 do not belong in knowledge-types.yaml or bounded-contexts.yaml: (1) key collision, mechanical and decisive — bounded-contexts.yaml already contains a 'governance' key (product-side, code_path app/Contexts/Governance), so adding D-1 'Engineering Governance' would collide with an existing key in a lint-enforced enum; (2) vocabulary insufficiency, strong — the domain model's verbs (governs, produces, consumes, validates, derives, depends on, observes) have no expression in the edge vocabulary (depends_on, derived_from, verified_by), which lacks governs/produces/consumes/observes; (3) subject mismatch, strong — every L-A field is a property of a document (knowledge_id, last_review, code_refs), but 'Engineering Method' has no reviewer, next-review date, or code refs, so it cannot carry a knowledge card. Verdict: D-1..D-7 belong to L-B (which does not yet exist); expressing them as data would require a separate vocabulary file with its own enum namespace, an ARB decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The five commissioned deliverables ... L-B ↔ L-A relationship | L-B would OWN and CLASSIFY L-A; L-A would never contain L-B
b_rows_sample.statement: L-B would own and classify L-A, never the reverse: L-A's subject is the document, L-B's subject is the platform — one is the metadata of artifacts, the other the architecture of the thing that produces them. The executable ontology should not change to accommodate L-B; two separately-warranted, ARB-only changes exist: whether scope.include should extend beyond docs/knowledge/** (a declared-scope amendment, not a bug fix), and whether the edge vocabulary needs governs/produces/consumes/observes, answerable only after L-B exists.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Package 4 — D-8 · Reconcile the three knowledge ontologies (blocks the same section)
b_rows_sample.statement: Package 4 (D-8): rule the scopes of L-A (executable, artifacts), the Metamodel (CANDIDATE, gate OQ-ENG-004), and RQ-002 (COMPLETE, dimensional) — one context, three competing models, per both reviews independently. Recommendation: ADOPT RQ-002 as the dimensional frame; scope the other two under it (L-A as its artifact projection; Metamodel proceeds to its own gate). Authority: ARB.

b_rows_sample.anchor: U-ONT-5 | Who owns the ontology? — same answer as U-MM-2: nobody
b_rows_sample.statement: U-ONT-5: who owns the ontology, recorded as nobody (same answer as U-MM-2) — waits on SA-1/sponsor layer.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 2 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: Known dimension, unknown value: P(expiry date|O). This is ordinary uncertainty about a known dimension. Unknown dimension: P(additional relevant dimension exists|O). This is uncertainty about the structure of the knowledge space. ... your point is primarily about the second one.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes two fundamentally different uncertainties: (1) known dimension, unknown value -- e.g. we know certificate expiry is relevant but not its date, P(expiry date|O), ordinary uncertainty about a known dimension; and (2) unknown dimension -- we don't know whether some additional dependency is relevant at all, P(additional relevant dimension exists|O), uncertainty about the structure of the knowledge space itself. Example: known dimensions (version, CPU, memory, repositories, network) may be well understood while other potential dimensions (identity integration, backup dependency, certificate dependency, licensing, external services, disaster recovery, operational dependency) remain undiscovered as even being relevant.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Person A knows 5 dimensions extremely well. Person B knows 20 dimensions reasonably well. ... B may have more knowledge because B has discovered a larger part of the relevant state space. ... Person C knows 5 dimensions extremely well and knows that there may be many undiscovered dimensions. Person C has less confidence in completeness, but arguably better epistemic awareness.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows why more information does not automatically mean more knowledge: Person A knows 5 dimensions extremely precisely; Person B knows 20 dimensions reasonably well and may have more knowledge overall by having discovered more of the relevant state space despite less precision per dimension; Person C knows 5 dimensions extremely well AND knows that many dimensions may remain undiscovered -- Person C has lower completeness confidence but arguably better epistemic awareness than either A or B.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "I think my knowledge is 95%." you may mean: P(we have identified the relevant dimensions sufficiently) approx 0.95. Not: P(each fact is correct)=0.95. ... Dimension coverage: 95%. Information accuracy: 99%. Reasoning confidence: 90%. These are three different epistemic properties.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the interpretation of a stated confidence like '95% knowledge': it likely means P(we have identified the relevant dimensions sufficiently) approx 0.95, not P(each fact is correct)=0.95 -- these are completely different quantities. Separates three distinct epistemic properties that a single percentage conflates: dimension coverage (e.g. 95%), information accuracy (e.g. 99%), and reasoning confidence (e.g. 90%).

a_rows_sample.anchor: D_t = relevant dimensions of the ideal state at time t. We don't know D_t completely. We have discovered: hat-D_t subset D_t. ... D_t -> hat-D_t: Which dimensions exist/relevant? and: I_t(hat-D_t) -> K_t: What do we know about those dimensions? The first is the dimension-discovery problem. The second is the state-extraction problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes D_t as the relevant dimensions of the ideal state at time t (not fully known), with hat-D_t subset D_t as the discovered subset, and observed information O_t(hat-D_t) about discovered dimensions; splits the problem into two: D_t -> hat-D_t (the dimension-discovery problem: which dimensions exist/are relevant) and I_t(hat-D_t) -> K_t (the state-extraction problem: what do we know about those dimensions).

a_rows_sample.anchor: P(D_t, I_t | O_{<=t}) is much closer to what you are describing than simply: P(F|O). We should not yet assume this exact mathematical formulation is correct. It is a research hypothesis.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes P(D_t,I_t|O_{<=t}) -- joint uncertainty over the dimension set AND the values within discovered dimensions -- as a richer formulation than the simple P(F|O), explicitly flagged as a research hypothesis not yet assumed correct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS cannot only store: "What do we know?" It must somehow preserve: "What dimensions of the subject do we currently believe are relevant?" and "How confident are we that our dimensional model is complete enough?" ... KnowledgeOS should potentially be able to say: "We have strong evidence concerning these dimensions, but there is unresolved uncertainty about whether additional relevant dimensions exist." That is a much more honest representation of knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS cannot only store 'what do we know' -- it must also preserve which dimensions are currently believed relevant and how confident the system is that its dimensional model is complete enough; without this, an AI could falsely claim 'I know everything about Nexus' when it has only modeled a handful of dimensions well. KnowledgeOS should instead be able to honestly say it has strong evidence on known dimensions but unresolved uncertainty about whether additional relevant dimensions exist.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Uncertainty begins not only when we don't know the value of something. It begins earlier -- when we don't know what things or dimensions are relevant to know about. ... Knowledge completeness = dimension coverage + information completeness within those dimensions, with uncertainty potentially existing at both levels.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the key insight simply: uncertainty begins not only when we don't know the value of something, but earlier -- when we don't know what dimensions are relevant to know about at all; therefore Knowledge completeness = dimension coverage + information completeness within those dimensions, with uncertainty potentially existing at both levels.

a_rows_sample.anchor: whether "dimension" is the right primitive at all, or whether what you are describing is more fundamentally a space of possible questions/propositions about the ideal state. That distinction could be decisive for the eventual mathematical model.
a_rows_sample.statement: Raises an open question that could be decisive for the eventual mathematical model: whether 'dimension' is the right primitive at all for this analysis, or whether what is being described is more fundamentally a space of possible questions/propositions about the ideal state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Few dimensions known / Many dimensions known x Little information per dimension / A lot of information per dimension -- Very low knowledge / Low-medium knowledge / Medium knowledge / High knowledge. But there is a crucial fifth question: How confident are we that we have discovered most of the relevant dimensions? So Knowledge may involve: Dimension Coverage x Information Quality x Determination Quality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Presents a 2x2 knowledge matrix crossing dimension count (few/many known) against information quality (little/a lot per dimension), yielding four qualitative knowledge levels (very low, low/medium, medium, high); adds a crucial fifth question -- confidence that most relevant dimensions have been discovered -- proposing conceptually (not yet as a formula) that Knowledge involves Dimension Coverage x Information Quality x Determination Quality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Team A knows version, CPU, RAM with extremely accurate information. Team B knows version, CPU, RAM, network, dependencies, certificates, backup, authentication, monitoring, licensing, but some of their information is uncertain. It is entirely possible that: Knowledge(B) > Knowledge(A) ... Because Team B has broader dimension coverage.
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: Team A knows only version/CPU/RAM but with extremely accurate information; Team B knows ten dimensions (version, CPU, RAM, network, dependencies, certificates, backup, authentication, monitoring, licensing) but some information is uncertain; despite Team A's higher per-dimension accuracy, Knowledge(B) > Knowledge(A) is entirely possible because Team B has broader dimension coverage.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Team A says: "We know 95% of the system." Team B says: "We know 70% of the system." But Team B has discovered that there may be unknown dimensions. ... Team B may actually possess better epistemic knowledge, because it knows what it does not know. ... known unknowns vs. unknown unknowns. But your formulation is more precise because you're talking about dimensions of the ideal state, not merely missing facts.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Team A/B example to a harder case: Team A claims 95% completeness with high confidence but low awareness of unknown dimensions, Team B claims only 70% completeness but has high awareness that unknown dimensions may exist; Team B may possess better epistemic knowledge because it knows what it does not know. Connects this to the known-unknowns/unknown-unknowns concept, but notes the present formulation is more precise since it concerns dimensions of the ideal state specifically, not merely missing facts in general.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A KnowledgeOS containing 10 million facts doesn't necessarily have more knowledge than one containing 1 million facts. ... Knowledge != Quantity of Information. Instead, at minimum: Knowledge ~ coverage of relevant dimensions + quality of information + confidence in completeness. Again, this is a research hypothesis, not yet a mathematical definition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues Knowledge cannot simply be measured by amount of stored information: a KnowledgeOS with 10 million facts about five dimensions need not have more knowledge than one with 1 million facts covering fifty dimensions -- Knowledge != Quantity of Information; instead, at minimum, Knowledge ~ coverage of relevant dimensions + quality of information + confidence in completeness, explicitly a research hypothesis, not yet a mathematical definition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Level 1 -- Value uncertainty: Is the installed version 2.69 or 2.70? P(X=2.69|O). Level 2 -- Structural/dimensional uncertainty: Have we identified all relevant aspects of the system? P(dimension coverage is complete|O). The second is much harder. And this is precisely where I would now be very careful about saying "measure theory solves it." ... we first need to establish what the random object actually is.
a_rows_sample.statement: Splits probability into two levels: Level 1, value uncertainty (e.g. P(X=2.69|O) -- is the installed version 2.69 or 2.70), and Level 2, structural/dimensional uncertainty (P(dimension coverage is complete|O) -- have all relevant aspects of the system been identified), the second being much harder; warns against casually claiming 'measure theory solves it' for Level 2 before establishing what the underlying random object actually is.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the observer may also need to estimate: D the space of dimensions in which that state should be described. So the problem becomes: First discover the relevant state space and then: Estimate the state within that space. ... Now we may need: P(D,X|O) where D=what dimensions are relevant; X=what values those dimensions have.
a_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes P(X|O) to P(D,X|O): an observer must jointly estimate the relevant dimension space D and the values X within it, not merely X alone -- first discover the relevant state space, then estimate the state within that space -- a much richer epistemic problem than previously formulated.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C_fact: confidence that a particular determination is correct. C_coverage: confidence that we have identified the relevant dimensions. C_model: confidence that our model of how those dimensions relate is correct. These are three different uncertainties.
a_rows_sample.statement: Separates three distinct confidence types that a single '90-95%' figure conflates: C_fact (confidence a particular determination is correct), C_coverage (confidence the relevant dimensions have been identified), and C_model (confidence the model of how those dimensions relate is correct).

a_rows_sample.anchor: IDEAL STATE -> (potentially many/infinite dimensions) -> Dimension discovery -> Which dimensions do we believe are relevant? -> State extraction -> What is the value/state of each known dimension? -> Determination -> KNOWLEDGE. And probability may potentially operate at both discovery and extraction levels.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives a pipeline diagram: IDEAL STATE (potentially many/infinite dimensions) -> Dimension discovery (which dimensions do we believe are relevant?) -> State extraction (what is the value/state of each known dimension?) -> Determination -> KNOWLEDGE; probability may operate at both the discovery and the extraction levels.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Not simply: "How accurately can we determine the state?" but: "How do we determine both the relevant dimensions of an ideal state and the state of those dimensions, given limited observation and reasoning capacity?" ... Dimension uncertainty + Value uncertainty + Temporal change + Comparative determination -- before we make any claim about what the KnowledgeOS Kernel must contain.
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the central research question from 'how accurately can we determine the state?' to 'how do we determine both the relevant dimensions of an ideal state and the state of those dimensions, given limited observation and reasoning capacity?'; sets the research concentration as Dimension uncertainty + Value uncertainty + Temporal change + Comparative determination, explicitly before any claim about what the KnowledgeOS Kernel must contain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: C_value: How confident are we about the values of known dimensions? C_coverage: How confident are we that we have identified the relevant dimensions? C_model: How confident are we that our model of relationships between those dimensions is correct? This suggests that "knowledge completeness" is not one number. It may be multidimensional.
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates dimension completeness as the newest and perhaps most important addition, formalizing three confidences C_value (values of known dimensions), C_coverage (identification of relevant dimensions), and C_model (correctness of the model of relationships between dimensions); suggests 'knowledge completeness' is not one number but potentially multidimensional -- a major insight, still a hypothesis.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The two hardest unresolved questions are now: 1. How is the relevant dimension space discovered? and: 2. What exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination? I would research those two questions next. And only after that would I return to measure theory and ask: Which parts of this process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability, and which do not? That prevents us from making the mathematics drive the ontology.
a_rows_sample.statement: Names the two hardest unresolved questions to research next: (1) how is the relevant dimension space discovered, and (2) what exactly constitutes a valid epistemic determination; only after resolving those should the research return to measure theory and ask which parts of the process genuinely require measure-theoretic probability and which do not -- explicitly to prevent the mathematics from driving the ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q1: What exactly is a "state"? ... Q2: Is every fact a dimension? ... Q3: Can dimensions themselves change? ... S_t -> S_{t+1} vs. D_t -> D_{t+1} ... Q4: What determines relevance of a dimension? Relevance(d | Context, Question, Purpose, Rules). But this is a hypothesis, not a definition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses four unresolved questions about the state/dimension ontology: Q1 what exactly is a 'state' (physical/software/business-process/institutional/propositional/knowledge-state, and can it contain entities/relationships/events/rules/capabilities/intentions/constraints); Q2 is every fact a dimension, or is the dimension-value pair distinct from the dimension itself, and does every relationship constitute a separate dimension; Q3 can dimensions themselves change (distinguishing state change S_t->S_{t+1} from dimension-model change D_t->D_{t+1}); Q4 what determines the relevance of a dimension, hypothesized as Relevance(d | Context, Question, Purpose, Rules) but not yet a definition. All marked Status: Undefined.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The corpus says 'nobody ever asked'. ... Seven of eight are directly covered; the eighth is partial. The audit reported zero of five.
b_rows_sample.statement: A six-way Zero-lens dimension/value taxonomy (known / unknown Zero-A / not-assessed / absent / not-applicable / unresolved Zero-B) with five non-collapse laws (UNKNOWN!=ABSENT, UNRESOLVED!=INVALID, NOT_ASSESSED!=LOW_CONFIDENCE, NOT_APPLICABLE!=UNKNOWN, NO_EVIDENCE!=INVALID_EVIDENCE) plus a sixth boxed law (UnknownValue(D)!=UnknownDimension(D)), together with an independently-committed Abhava ontological absence typology (Pragabhava/Pradhvamsabhava/Atyantabhava/Anyonyabhava) and an AbsenceClaim record shape, jointly cover seven of the mandate's eight missingness cases directly and one partially -- versus the audit's report of zero of five covered.

b_rows_sample.anchor: There is no component of K holding the set of recognised dimensions. ... D_t is the smallest missing component. With it, 'not assessed' is D in D_t AND not exists a in A: a.P.D=D -- decidable in O(n). Without it, the statement has no truth-maker.
b_rows_sample.statement: An executed probe (MISSINGNESS-NOT-ASSESSED in THEORY-CONSTRUCTION-TEST.md) shows a never-assessed dimension and an assessed-with-no-result dimension both render identically in K=(A,R) as 'no assertion mentioning that dimension', proving them provably indistinguishable; introducing D_t (the set of currently recognised dimensions) as a component of K makes 'not assessed' decidable in O(n) and is identified as the smallest missing component to close the missingness gap.

b_rows_sample.anchor: VERIFIER RECOMMENDS -- not CORPUS ESTABLISHES. K = (D_t, A, R) ... with id = H(P, e_refs, c, t, Pi) where e_refs projects out the mutable state. ... Nothing here is adopted. This is a proposal, and it is smaller than the three the corpus already contains -- which should be consumed first (ES-005.4).
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes (explicitly labelled VERIFIER RECOMMENDS, not adopted) a minimal repair K=(D_t,A,R) adding the recognised-dimension set D_t and redefining id=H(P,e_refs,c,t,Pi) to project out the mutable state field, arguing this closes the missingness gap (7/8 cases), removes the identity/mutability contradiction, and makes a dedup operator definable by unioning Pi and e on (P,c,t); explicitly states this does not repair non-identifiability (needs a W,Omega layer beneath K) or uncertainty (needs U(H)), and that the corpus's own existing three constructions should be consumed first per ES-005.4.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Empty != ContradictoryEvidence. ... Missing != False. ... EvalPolicy may need a third result: Undetermined.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues no-evidence must be distinguished from conflicting-evidence when assigning Sigma=Unknown, and that a missing required measurement (x=?) cannot be inferred as False; proposes a candidate three-valued policy-decision output {Permit, Deny, Undetermined} as a bridge between missingness and policy, explicitly marked as a candidate requiring corpus confirmation, not a final decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The three exclusions were a discovery failure, not a mathematical limit. They are absent from the AUTHORIZED MODEL v0.2 ... so the finding is real, and it is a GOVERNANCE finding: the constructions exist and were never promoted.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a prior verdict ('THEORY CLOSED AGAINST THE STATED CRITERIA -- NOT COMPLETE IN EVERY RESPECT', with 'a theory that cannot say nobody ever asked is closed, not finished') by showing the corpus does say 'nobody ever asked' (the not-assessed Zero-lens dimension state, committed one day before this programme began) and does have formal, typed constructions for non-identifiability and uncertainty; reclassifies the three exclusions as a discovery failure rather than a mathematical limit, and as a governance finding since these constructions are measured absent (zero grep occurrences of unknown/absent/not assessed/uncertain/identifiab) from the authorized v0.2 model despite existing in the raw corpus.

b_rows_sample.anchor: - **`Missingness` — 0.**
b_rows_sample.statement: Three concepts have exactly zero definitional occurrences corpus-wide: Missingness (the concept exists richly under other names — Zero, abhāva, Missing, 'not assessed' — so this is a vocabulary gap masquerading as a theory gap), Admissibility (its two laws are cited constantly, 42.9/42.41, but the term itself is never defined), and AuthorityAct (confirming, by whole-corpus scan rather than targeted grep, that the object the entire governance model turns on has no type).

b_rows_sample.anchor:
**First, the vocabulary fact that explains why this looked unresolved:** the word **`Missingness`
 has 0 definitional occurrences corpus-wide**
b_rows_sample.statement: 8 of 9 mandated missingness distinctions (not-asked, asked-but-no-answer, unknown, absent, no-evidence-found, searched-but-insufficient, deliberately-omitted, deleted; only 'never existed'/Prāgabhāva lacks one) have a named corpus construct across the Zero taxonomy and the Sanskrit abhāva typology, and 4 of them (unknown, absent, insufficient, not-applicable) are executable, tested, passing code in zero_reference.py (8/8 tests); the word 'Missingness' itself has 0 definitional occurrences, so searching for the word finds nothing while the capability exists richly under other names.

b_rows_sample.anchor: With D_t: "not assessed" is D ∈ D_t ∧ ¬∃a ∈ 𝒜 : a.P.D = D — decidable in O(n).
b_rows_sample.statement: The Zero model's D_t (recognised-dimension set) plus Z_t=Omega\Represented(K_t) layer, already present in the corpus, makes 'not assessed' a decidable O(n) predicate (D in D_t and no assertion covers D), and this is proposed as the minimum additional structural component needed -- not invented, but recovered from the corpus's own Zero-lens construction.

b_notations: not assessed / absent / not applicable / unresolved

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels share the notation 'D_t'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Merge(K_A,K_B,K_C) becomes fundamental
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the model to multiple knowledge producers (KnowledgeOS instances A, B and a Human/Agent C each observing different parts of the world), requiring a general Merge(K_A,K_B,K_C) operation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_A: Nexus=3.69, K_B: Nexus=3.70 ... merge must determine Equivalent? TemporalEvolution? Contradiction? IndependentEvidence? Authority?
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects a naive 'A+B=combined knowledge' model: differing values require the merge to determine equivalence, temporal evolution, contradiction, independent-evidence status, and authority rather than arbitrarily picking one.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Merge(K_A,K_B) must not flatten everything into one anonymous record ... assertion/support/provenance/temporal relations/conflicts
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires merged knowledge to retain Origin(K_A) and Origin(K_B) rather than flattening into an anonymous record, illustrated with a structured merged-knowledge sketch (assertion, support per source, provenance, temporal relations, conflicts).

a_rows_sample.anchor: RecordID_A\neq RecordID_B ... Evidence_A\neq Evidence_B ... KAID_A=KAID_B ... exactly why we introduced Knowledge Meaning Identity
a_rows_sample.statement: Independent systems reaching the same conclusion have different RecordIDs and Evidence but may share Knowledge Atma meaning identity (KAID_A=KAID_B) — explicitly the reason the Meaning/Record identity split was introduced.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Merge can unify semantic identity (KAID_A=KAID_B) while preserving multiple epistemic records (Record_A\neq Record_B) ... correct model for independent corroboration
a_rows_sample.statement: States merge has two simultaneous effects: unifying semantic identity while preserving multiple distinct epistemic records — 'the correct model for independent corroboration.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic deduplication must not mean provenance deduplication ... statistically this can be disastrous
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that naive deduplication discarding provenance loses the fact that two independent observations supported an assertion — statistically disastrous — 'semantic deduplication must not mean provenance deduplication.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: H_{merge}=H_A\cup H_B ... K_{merge}=Derive(H_{merge},\Omega,EC,M) ... much cleaner than directly merging opaque states
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes merging at the event-history level (H_merge=H_A∪H_B, subject to identity/causal rules) then deriving K_merge=Derive(H_merge,Omega,EC,M), 'much cleaner than directly merging opaque states.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: EventID ... E_1=E_2 can be detected ... EventIdentity\rightarrow DuplicateDetection
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires EventID (global unique or deterministic content-derived identity) to detect duplicate event transmission — EventIdentity -> DuplicateDetection.

a_rows_sample.anchor: identical events are not necessarily independent ... Independent(E_1,E_2)=False ... Replication is not new evidence
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that a replicated copy of an event is not independent evidence: Independent(E1,E2)=False when E2 is a replica of E1 — 'replication is not new evidence' — requiring OriginEventID preservation through replication.

a_rows_sample.anchor: E_1\rightarrow E_2 causal ... Observation->LLM interpretation->Human decision ... A merge must preserve them
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example of a causal event chain (observation -> LLM interpretation -> human decision) that a merge must preserve as causally related, not merely temporally ordered.

a_rows_sample.anchor: E_1\prec E_2 causally precedes ... stronger than Timestamp(E_1)<Timestamp(E_2)
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes causal ordering (E1≺E2) from wall-clock timestamp ordering, since distributed clocks can differ; suggests CausalRelation or logical clocks as needed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: event IDs; causal ordering; logical clocks; append-only event streams; idempotent consumers; version vectors ... epistemic model sits on top of these mechanisms
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS does not need to reinvent distributed systems — it reuses established mechanisms (event IDs, causal ordering, logical clocks, append-only streams, idempotent consumers, version vectors), with the epistemic model layered on top — 'another important architectural result.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_A'\equiv K_B' provided both have received the same relevant information and use the same \Omega,EC,M ... convergence
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines convergence: after synchronization, K_A'≡K_B' provided both nodes share the same Omega, EC, M and relevant event information.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H_A=H_B and \Omega_A=\Omega_B and EC_A=EC_B and M_A=M_B implies Derive(H_A,...)\equiv Derive(H_B,...) ... extremely desirable
a_rows_sample.statement: States a candidate convergence theorem: identical event sets, ontology, contract, and assessment model across two instances implies semantically equivalent derived KnowledgeStates — 'extremely desirable,' and separately argues it means KnowledgeOS does not require 'one magical central brain,' fitting enterprise architecture with independently-maintained-then-converging bounded contexts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Node A: H_A={E1,E2}, Node B: H_B={E2,E3} ... H_A'=H_B'={E1,E2,E3} ... K_A'=K_B'
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: two nodes with partially overlapping event sets converge to the same union and, under a deterministic derivation model, the same derived knowledge state.

a_rows_sample.anchor:
E_1\vdash A and E_2\vdash
eg A ... both should converge to Conflict(A,
eg A) ... AgreementOnEpistemicState, not AgreementOnTruth ... Convergence
eq Consensus
a_rows_sample.statement: States that conflict does not prevent convergence: both nodes eventually receiving both contradictory events should converge to the same Conflict(A,¬A) state; convergence means AgreementOnEpistemicState, not AgreementOnTruth, giving Convergence ≠ Consensus — 'exactly appropriate for epistemic systems,' distinct from distributed-systems consensus (deciding which assertion is true).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Merge\rightarrow\{Agreement,Conflict,Unresolved,Independent\}
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines four possible merged-relationship outcomes: Agreement (mutually supported), Conflict (A⊥B), Unresolved relation (insufficient semantics to determine), and Independent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H_1\sqcup H_2=H_1\cup H_2 ... commutative, associative, idempotent ... CRDT-like thinking
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws a CRDT analogy: an append-only immutable event set behaves like a grow-only structure under union, satisfying idempotence (H∪H=H), commutativity (H1∪H2=H2∪H1), and associativity ((H1∪H2)∪H3=H1∪(H2∪H3)) — 'extremely attractive,' contrasted with S0902's explicit refusal to grant these properties to knowledge-merge in general.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EventHistory can be monotonic while DerivedKnowledge can be non-monotonic ... This is actually ideal
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates and reinforces the event-history/derived-knowledge separation in the distributed setting: EventHistory can be monotonic (CRDT-like union) while DerivedKnowledge (incorporating temporal state, retractions, conflict resolution, authority, policy, model versions) can be non-monotonic — 'this is actually ideal' since it separates distributed convergence from epistemic semantics.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A records E_1:Version=3.70, later E_2:Retract(E_1) ... K_A may say Retracted while K_B still says Supported ... not necessarily inconsistency
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked distributed-retraction example: a node that has not yet received a retraction event legitimately differs from one that has, without this being inconsistency — convergence follows once the retraction event propagates.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can KnowledgeOS compute K_{t+1} from K_t and new evidence? ... K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_t,\Omega,EC)
b_rows_sample.statement: States the central question of the step and defines the fundamental transition function K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,E_t,Omega,EC) where K_t=current state, E_t=new epistemic input, Omega=domain ontology/rules, EC=applicable epistemic contract.

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x EpistemicInput x Ontology x EpistemicContract

b_rows_sample.anchor: K=(Assertions,Evidence,Provenance,Relations,Assessments,Validity,TemporalState,Conflicts,Versions,Contracts,Policies)
b_rows_sample.statement: Rejects K={facts} in favor of an 11-component tuple K=(Assertions, Evidence, Provenance, Relations, Assessments, Validity, TemporalState, Conflicts, Versions, Contracts, Policies), with Decisions/Actions/Observations optionally included depending on whether event history is treated as part of state or an external log.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeState=DerivedState ... EventLog=HistoricalCause ... an important DDD distinction
b_rows_sample.statement: Recommends keeping the event log conceptually separate from the derived KnowledgeState: Events_t and K_t=Fold(Events_0..t), giving KnowledgeState=DerivedState vs EventLog=HistoricalCause — 'an important DDD distinction.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: 10:00 Nexus=3.69, 11:00 Nexus=3.70, 12:00 Nexus=3.70 ... CurrentKnowledge\neq HistoricalKnowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: a three-event history where the current state (3.70) differs from the full history (3.69->3.70), showing both are valuable — CurrentKnowledge ≠ HistoricalKnowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: DeterministicUpdate ... our first major invariant
b_rows_sample.statement: States the first invariant: for fixed (K_t,E_t,Omega,EC), Update must produce the same K_{t+1} on repeated execution — DeterministicUpdate.

b_rows_sample.anchor: RawInput\rightarrow LLM\rightarrow CandidateEvidence ... NonDeterministicAcquisition\rightarrow GovernedInput\rightarrow DeterministicStateTransition
b_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the LLM-nondeterminism concern: an LLM may participate before admission (RawInput->LLM->CandidateEvidence), but once admitted as a structured event E_t the transition is deterministic — 'one of the most important architectural boundaries we have discovered.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Update(Update(K,E),E)\equiv Update(K,E) ... idempotence
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the second invariant, idempotence: applying the same evidence twice should not create artificial additional knowledge, Update(Update(K,E),E) ≡ Update(K,E), worked with a duplicate-database-record example resolved via EvidenceID(E1)=EvidenceID(E2) duplicate detection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Update must never destroy the source lineage ... Provenance(K)\supseteq Provenance(E)
b_rows_sample.statement: States the third invariant, provenance preservation: after E->A->K, Provenance(K) ⊇ Provenance(E) — 'Update must be provenance-preserving.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: UnresolvedConflict\rightarrow UnresolvedConflict unless new evidence or governance explicitly resolves it
b_rows_sample.statement: States the fourth invariant, contradiction preservation: contradictory same-time/context evidence with no resolution rule must remain an unresolved conflict rather than being silently resolved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: NoImplicitConflictResolution ... must not create A or B as the uniquely accepted truth merely because one looks more likely
b_rows_sample.statement: States the fifth invariant, no hallucinated resolution: given A⊥B with no authorized resolution rule, Update must not pick a winner because it 'looks more likely' — NoImplicitConflictResolution.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t\subseteq K_{t+1} ... not always true ... naive monotonicity fails
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests naive monotonicity (K_t⊆K_{t+1}) against a version-change example (3.69->3.70 changes current state) and finds it fails.

b_rows_sample.anchor: H_t\subseteq H_{t+1} ... History is monotonic; CurrentState need not be
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the sixth invariant into event-sourced monotonicity: historical event knowledge H_t is monotonic (events accumulate, history is never erased) even though current derived state is not — 'History is monotonic; CurrentState need not be' — 'a much better formulation.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: H_{t+1}=H_t\cup\{E_t\} ... K_{t+1}=Derive(H_{t+1},\Omega,EC) ... elegant
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes the two-layer transition: H_{t+1}=H_t ∪ {E_t} (monotonic history growth) then K_{t+1}=Derive(H_{t+1},Omega,EC) (current state recomputation) — 'elegant.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Retract(E_1) ... Status(E_1)=Retracted ... K_{current} is recalculated
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines retraction: a source's later 'the previous record was incorrect' becomes Retract(E1), setting Status(E1)=Retracted (not deleting E1 from history), then recalculating K_current.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_2:Correction(E_1,3.69) ... preserve E_1 and record E_2 ... Correction\neq Deletion
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines correction as distinct from retraction/deletion: E2=Correction(E1,3.69) preserves E1 while recording the correcting event E2; the derived state may change to 3.69 — 'Correction ≠ Deletion.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: The certificate used to establish the evidence has been revoked ... EvidenceValidity(E)=False ... Assertion separate from EvidenceAssessment
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines revocation: a source can become invalid (e.g. a revoked certificate) without the proposition itself being false, EvidenceValidity(E)=False while the assertion remains historically recorded — demonstrates Assertion must be kept separate from EvidenceAssessment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ValidFrom\le t<ValidUntil ... Expired\neq False
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines explicit validity intervals; when t>=ValidUntil the knowledge becomes Expired, explicitly distinct from False — 'this distinction is extremely important.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: True/Supported, False/Refuted, Unknown, Expired, Conflicted ... must not be collapsed into a single Boolean
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists (at least) five epistemic states that must not be collapsed into a single Boolean: Supported, Refuted, Unknown, Expired, and potentially Conflicted.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal E=\{Unknown,Supported,Refuted,Conflicted,Expired,Retracted\} ... I would not yet call this a simple lattice ... Expired does not necessarily mean Refuted
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a six-state epistemic space E={Unknown,Supported,Refuted,Conflicted,Expired,Retracted} but explicitly declines to call it a simple lattice since some states are orthogonal dimensions (Expired does not imply Refuted; Retracted may concern evidence rather than assertion).

b_rows_sample.anchor: EpistemicState=(SupportStatus,ValidityStatus,ConflictStatus,TemporalStatus) ... much more expressive
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the epistemic-state space into a four-dimension tuple EpistemicState=(SupportStatus,ValidityStatus,ConflictStatus,TemporalStatus), worked with two example instantiations (one with ConflictStatus=none, one with ConflictStatus=conflicted) — 'much more expressive.'

a_aliases: Distributed Knowledge, Merge, Convergence and Consistency

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'distributed-knowledge-merge-convergence-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'knowledge-state-closure-algebra' (batch B0022). Note: S0904's Step 25L: extends the S0903 closure/state-machine model to multiple independent producers, establishing a convergence theorem candidate, CRDT-analogy for event-history union, and bounded-context-relative ontology/metaknowledge treatment; distinct from but directly dependent on knowledge-state-closure-algebra (S0903) and knowledge-identity-atma-algebra (S0901).

a_rows_sample.anchor: EKS is presently a governance-oriented engineering knowledge system whose primary durable knowledge representation is repository-based YAML/Markdown ... Its conceptual model is more mature than its executable software implementation.
a_rows_sample.statement: States this document's strongest current-state summary sentence for EKS, explicitly refusing to describe it as a mature microservice platform, event-driven knowledge graph, or PostgreSQL-centered product.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the certified PKS documents explicitly state that the PKS is knowledge specifications in YAML + Markdown and does not require PHP, Python, or another programming language, while other documents describe PHP/Laravel/PostgreSQL software ... this baseline does not resolve that contradiction artificially.
a_rows_sample.statement: Records an unresolved contradiction between the certified 'PKS is not software' position and later PHP/Laravel/PostgreSQL descriptions, deliberately preserved rather than reconciled.

a_rows_sample.anchor: G0 PKS 'documentation/instruction system' → self-correction → G1 PKS knowledge system YAML+Markdown+Git → G2 KnowledgeOS proposal 6 bounded contexts → G3 EKS proposal 7 contexts→4 contexts+planes PostgreSQL-centric → G3/v3 reconciliation returns to: repository system of record.
a_rows_sample.statement: Traces four successive historical architecture 'generations' of PKS/EKS/KnowledgeOS naming and positioning, showing a reversal from a certified repository-as-system-of-record position through a PostgreSQL-centric proposal and back to a repository-centric reconciliation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The current C4 CONTESTED / Target C4 diagrams PROPOSED ... Do not use them as evidence for current runtime boundaries.
a_rows_sample.statement: Concludes there is no authoritative current C4 container model for EKS; several competing-generation C4 diagrams exist and must not be read as evidence of current runtime boundaries.

a_rows_sample.anchor: scripts should first be understood as mechanisms and capabilities, not directly mapped into services or bounded contexts.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against mapping existing scripts directly to services/bounded contexts, treating them instead as a capability inventory (Workflow engine → governance/execution mechanism, Session resolver → workflow infrastructure, etc.).

a_rows_sample.anchor: The mechanism records authority; it does not grant authority ... All 20/20 grants carry humanActRef, and registeredBy has exactly one observed value — governance.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the highest-confidence current-state finding of this EKS baseline: measured directly from 9 work items and 20 grants, every grant references a human act and is registered by governance, evidencing that the mechanism records rather than creates authority.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Grants with validity information 0/20 ... Grants with delegation information 0/20 ... Grants with ownership information 0/20 ... Was this authority valid at a particular historical point in time? ... a current-state limitation, not a future-architecture opinion.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the principal measured weakness: authority is durably recorded but the record contains no validity/delegation/ownership fields, so historical authority cannot be reliably reconstructed at any past point in time.

a_rows_sample.anchor: An AI agent must not be interpreted as an authority holder merely because it executes a permitted activity.
a_rows_sample.statement: States that AI-process participation is current infrastructure, but permitted execution must not be confused with holding authority, following directly from the observed authority model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would not yet call 'Delegation modelling' IMPLEMENTED-BUT-IMPLICIT merely from the progressive narrowing of grants ... change it to: OBSERVED BEHAVIOUR — SEMANTIC INTERPRETATION UNKNOWN.
a_rows_sample.statement: A second-session self-critique downgrades an earlier classification: observed progressive grant-narrowing behaviour does not establish that the business concept 'Delegation' exists in EKS, so the classification must be weakened to avoid treating an interpretation as an architectural fact.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would also weaken: Rule governance — PARTIAL ... because that potentially mixes exploratory Track 2 Rule semantics with the current EKS implementation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns that classifying 'Rule governance' as PARTIAL risks importing the exploratory Track-2 Rule Model's semantics into a current-state EKS claim, and proposes the safer statement that Rule-like mechanisms exist while the Track-2 model itself is not established as current architecture.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EKS turns engineering activity into evidence, evidence into bounded recommendations and decisions, and decisions into durable engineering knowledge — while keeping architectural authority with humans and keeping future architectural evolution evidence-gated.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the single strongest coherent description of the current EKS architecture that this document's evidence supports, offered as the closing summary of a 60-section baseline.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Behavioral governance demonstrated (tier 5 record): the governance changed real contributor behavior (a new artifact written instead of amending a frozen one) even where the automated gate was absent — 'tool enforcement says you COULDN'T; behavioral governance says you COULD have, and you didn't.'
a_rows_sample.statement: Cites a demonstrated case where governance discipline changed contributor behavior even without a mechanical enforcement gate, distinguishing tool-enforced impossibility from behavioral-governance restraint.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This document establishes a CURRENT ARCHITECTURE BASELINE. It does not authorize: redesign; refactoring; bounded-context creation; service extraction; event-bus introduction; platform extraction; adaptive learning; technology migration.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the baseline's own authority boundary and the seven-value classification vocabulary (CURRENT/IMPLEMENTED-BUT-IMPLICIT/PARTIAL/DOCUMENTED-ONLY/HISTORICAL/PROPOSED/UNKNOWN) that any future proposal evaluated against it must use.

a_rows_sample.anchor: whether EKS and PKS are the same system, different systems, or overlapping systems is UNRESOLVED by PKS evidence (§24 U-02).
a_rows_sample.statement: Leaves the PKS/EKS identity relationship explicitly UNRESOLVED from PKS evidence alone, refusing to import EKS semantics to close the ambiguity per the study's amendment 4.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the EKS baseline is BROKEN / INCOMPLETE (ends at §20; §21–§25 absent; U-/X- registers missing). Therefore 'EKS does not evidence X' is recorded as UNKNOWN (incomplete corpus), never as NOT-PRESENT.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies a binding evidence-completeness discipline given a discovered defect in a prior-phase deliverable (the EKS Stage-1 baseline is missing its final five sections and registers): an absence in an incomplete corpus must be recorded as UNKNOWN, never conflated with a positive absence finding.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the real double-evaluation defect in current systems is EKS's three LCOM4 implementations — one semantic concern evaluated by three independent mechanisms with no canonical choice.
a_rows_sample.statement: Tests CAPPI's orthogonality/double-dampening warning against the estate and finds the real analog is not a reliability-vs-uncertainty conflation but a triple redundant implementation of one cohesion measurement (three independent LCOM4 collectors) with no canonical winner.

b_rows_sample.anchor: CONFIDENCE ≠ AUTHORITY is the strongest-supported external principle ... EKS (AP-1) ... PKS (AP-1; promotion is a distinct Authority act) ... AIP (produced records ≠ owned authority) all implement or imply the separation.
b_rows_sample.statement: H-02: the strongest-supported external epistemic principle tested against all three baselines — analytical confidence and organizational authority are separately implemented or governed concepts — ESTABLISHED in EKS/PKS, PARTIALLY ESTABLISHED in AIP.

b_rows_sample.anchor: CAPPI's numeric epistemic stack (mu/tau/w -> Bayesian fusion -> quality score) has ZERO current-architecture support. None of EKS/PKS/AIP uses a continuous calibrated confidence signal, a Bayesian fusion step, or a scalar quality score.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reports the single strongest case in the investigation of an elegant external principle unsupported by current evidence: continuous calibrated confidence, per-instance uncertainty, and a reliability weight (mu/tau/w) are absent from all three baselines, whose discrete verdict vocabularies and honest UNKNOWN answers are philosophically the inverse of a probabilistic quality score.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the EKS baseline is BROKEN / INCOMPLETE (ends at §20; §21–§25 absent; U-/X- registers missing). Therefore 'EKS does not evidence X' is recorded as UNKNOWN (incomplete corpus), never as NOT-PRESENT.
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies a binding evidence-completeness discipline given a discovered defect in a prior-phase deliverable (the EKS Stage-1 baseline is missing its final five sections and registers): an absence in an incomplete corpus must be recorded as UNKNOWN, never conflated with a positive absence finding.

b_rows_sample.anchor: C-1 Authority-as-recorded-reference-to-a-human-act ... C-2 State-as-fold ... C-3 Closed-verdict-vocabulary as published language ... C-4 Assessment-conferring-no-authority ... C-5 Forward-only supersession ... C-6 Per-kind register-scoped identity ... C-7 Regenerable non-authoritative projection ... C-10 Honest-UNKNOWN as first-class answer.
b_rows_sample.statement: Registers eight KERNEL-CANDIDATE concepts (of ten total, with C-8/C-9 classified differently), each with cross-system evidence in at least two of EKS/PKS/AIP, a shared invariant, and a stable lifecycle, but explicitly notes none is promoted — only that each has enough evidence to warrant the AMENDMENT-6 kernel-candidate progression.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the closest real-world analog of the CAPPI fallback risk is not in any system's code but in the P3-F1 incident: an unread evidence artifact was declared 'not needed' — a silent epistemic-status change.
b_rows_sample.statement: Finds that EKS/PKS/AIP are all anti-fallback/fail-closed by design at the code level, so the CAPPI fallback-chain risk's real analog in this estate is a documentation-level failure mode: treating unavailable evidence as irrelevant is itself a silent shift from 'known' to 'assumed.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: Claim/Interpretation and Confidence are NOT PRESENT as named concepts. The systems use discrete verdicts and honest UNKNOWN instead of a confidence scalar. Whether the KnowledgeOS pipeline needs these stages is UNKNOWN.
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests the proposed Observation/Evidence/Claim/Confidence/Authority/Decision pipeline stage by stage against all three baselines; Observation, Evidence, Authority, and Decision are real but system-specific concepts, while Claim/Interpretation and Confidence exist nowhere as named first-class concepts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the real double-evaluation defect in current systems is EKS's three LCOM4 implementations — one semantic concern evaluated by three independent mechanisms with no canonical choice.
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests CAPPI's orthogonality/double-dampening warning against the estate and finds the real analog is not a reliability-vs-uncertainty conflation but a triple redundant implementation of one cohesion measurement (three independent LCOM4 collectors) with no canonical winner.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Consistency is determined by invariant ownership, not by whether communication is event-driven ... established for the non-distributed current context; generalization UNKNOWN.
b_rows_sample.statement: H-08: tests whether invariant ownership (not event-driven architecture) is what actually produces consistency in all three systems; PARTIALLY ESTABLISHED because none of the three systems is distributed, so whether ownership alone suffices under distribution remains unproven.

b_rows_sample.anchor: effective_from/effective_until/superseded_at exist nowhere ... Temporal knowledge is the least-supported element of the proposed kernel boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Finds that none of EKS/PKS/AIP records decided_at, effective_from, effective_until, or superseded_at timestamps (2/218 and 2/218 transitions dated in EKS/AIP; PKS has forward-only supersession as a concept but no timestamps), making the temporal-state kernel concern the weakest-supported of seven proposed kernel concerns.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KNOWLEDGEOS KERNEL protects: identity · evidence · provenance · lifecycle · authority · invariants · temporal state / higher layers provide: assurance · analytics · inference · simulation · AI · visualization · delivery ... a PROPOSED KERNEL BOUNDARY CANDIDATE, outline supported, provenance+temporal weak.
b_rows_sample.statement: H-10: tests the seven-concern kernel/higher-layer split against all three baselines per-concern; identity, evidence, lifecycle, authority, and invariants are supported, provenance and temporal state are weak, so the overall split is a candidate outline, not an established fact.

b_rows_sample.anchor: R-1 — Complete the EKS evidence corpus (UNBLOCKING) ... Without this, every 'EKS does not evidence X' is UNKNOWN ... R-2 ... R-3 — AMENDMENT 6 kernel-candidate progression for C-1..C-10 ... R-7 — DDD validation phase.
b_rows_sample.statement: Issues a seven-item dependency-ordered research agenda (R-1..R-7), starting with completing the broken EKS evidence corpus as the precondition unblocking HPA re-review, Stage-4 Landscape, kernel-candidate promotion testing, orthogonality/temporal/fallback studies, and eventual DDD validation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Do not merge concepts merely because names match: confidence, reliability, authority are NOT one thing ... Evidence in EKS (5 senses) is not the same concept as Evidence in PKS (governed substrate).
b_rows_sample.statement: Closing DDD discipline: applies the name-collision-is-not-concept-equality rule across all three baselines' overloaded vocabulary (Evidence, Decision, Session, Authority), refusing to infer identity from shared terminology alone.

a_rows_sample.statement: Argues against a naive lift-and-shift of EKS code into a kernel package, proposing instead a capability-by-capability kernel-worthiness classification.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Kernel criterion 1: Would PKS need it? ... Kernel criterion 6: Can EKS depend on it without the kernel depending on EKS?
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes six kernel-worthiness criteria (cross-domain need, future-domain need, own invariant, stable lifecycle, engineering-independence, and the dependency-direction test that the kernel must never depend on EKS).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Artifact existence ≠ Authority ... Record existence ≠ Authority establishment. That is exactly the kind of invariant a kernel can protect.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes generalizing the existing EKS Authority invariant (record ≠ authority) into a kernel-level Authority mechanism owning principal/scope/capability/grant/lifecycle/evidence, with domain-specific 'which architecture is correct' judgement left above the kernel.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EKS should initially become a Kernel Adapter / Domain Module ... EKS becomes the first major domain implementation running on KnowledgeOS kernel primitives.
a_rows_sample.statement: Recommends framing EKS not as becoming the kernel, but as the first domain module running on kernel primitives extracted from it, avoiding the terminology 'EKS becomes the KnowledgeOS kernel.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: the current baseline explicitly says that bounded contexts are not yet sufficiently demonstrated as current implementation boundaries. Therefore I would not yet create KnowledgeOS::GovernanceContext ...
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against freezing final bounded contexts before an 'EKS → KnowledgeOS Kernel Extraction & Conformance Analysis' has been run, proposing that dedicated investigation as the next assignment instead.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the existing EKS is evidence for the kernel design. We shouldn't invent a kernel first and then ask how to migrate EKS into it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the kernel-design approach: extract kernel primitives from evidence of what EKS already implements, rather than designing a kernel independently and then retrofitting EKS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ChangeSet may be a particularly important kernel abstraction ... it potentially belongs below EKS ... EKS collectors / PKS collectors
